items.hint1: This is about the law that controls who may use land in Nigeria. Think about how long the right of use lasts on the document the government issues.
items.hint2: The Land Use Act of 1978 places land in each state under the governor. A person gets a right to use land, shown by a certificate of occupancy, for a fixed term rather than forever.
items.hint3: The two short terms are not the figure taught for this certificate. Between the two long terms, recall the maximum term normally linked with a statutory certificate of occupancy.
items.solution:
Answer: C. 99 years

Under Nigeria's Land Use Act of 1978, land in each state is held by the governor in trust for the people. A person does not own the land outright but gets a right to use it, shown by a certificate of occupancy. The Act says this right is for a definite term, and in practice, as the syllabus teaches, a statutory right of occupancy is granted for up to 99 years.

How to tell: the certificate gives a long, fixed right of use, like a very long lease. The term normally given, and the one the syllabus teaches, is up to 99 years.

Why not the others:
A. 20 years: not the term taught for a statutory certificate of occupancy.
B. 59 years: not the term taught for a statutory certificate of occupancy.
D. 100 years: a round figure that sounds right, but the usual maximum term is 99 years.

Exam tip: for land law questions, link the Land Use Act to three facts: 1978, the governor holds the land in trust, and the certificate of occupancy normally runs for up to 99 years.

items.hint1: Ask yourself why some farm produce is plentiful at one time of year and scarce at another. What natural factor controls when most crops can grow?
items.hint2: In West Africa most crops are planted with the rains, so harvests come in one season. To remove seasonality, farmers must be able to produce outside the rainy season, not just teach, tend or sell differently.
items.hint3: Exporting only moves produce that already exists, so set that aside. Of the rest, ask which one removes the farmer's need to wait for rain.
items.solution:
Answer: A. practicing irrigation

Seasonality means produce is plentiful at harvest and scarce later, because most crops in West Africa are grown with the rains. Irrigation supplies water in the dry season, so crops can be planted and harvested at other times of the year and supply becomes more even. In the syllabus, irrigation is the standard answer for evening out seasonal production.

How to tell: the cause of seasonality is dependence on rainfall. Irrigation is the option that directly reduces that dependence, by bringing water to the crop when there is no rain.

Why not the others:
B. better extension services: extension teaches farmers better methods, but on its own it does not let them grow crops without rain.
C. employing cultural cultivation practices: weeding, mulching and similar practices help crops and can stretch the growing period a little, but they do not supply water for growing crops right through the dry season.
D. exportation during scare periods: sending produce out when it is already scarce makes local scarcity worse and does not change when crops are produced.

Exam tip: irrigation evens out production, while storage and processing even out supply after harvest. For a question about removing seasonality of production, pick the option that lets crops grow out of season.

items.hint1: Think about what agricultural research tries to give farmers: crops that are better than the ones they had before.
items.hint2: Research aims at improvements such as higher yield, better quality, resistance to pests and diseases, and early maturity. Any option that makes a crop weaker cannot be a benefit of research.
items.hint3: Two options describe crops that pests or diseases attack more easily, so they are harmful. Between keeping old local varieties and breeding new ones, which is an improvement?
items.solution:
Answer: B. develops crops that short maturity period

Agricultural research breeds improved crop varieties. One of its main aims is early maturity, meaning crops that are ready for harvest sooner, so the farmer can harvest earlier, escape late drought or pests, and sometimes grow two crops in a year.

How to tell: a correct answer to a why research matters question describes an improvement. A shorter maturity period is an improvement. The other options make crops weaker or leave them unimproved.

Why not the others:
A. promotes the use of local varieties of crops: using local varieties as they are does not by itself bring new improvements such as early maturity or higher yield, although local varieties are often used as parents in breeding.
C. develops crops that are susceptible to local diseases: susceptible means easily attacked, the opposite of what research wants.
D. produces crops with reduced resistance to pests: research aims to raise resistance to pests, not lower it.

Exam tip: in questions on the aims of research or crop improvement, pick the option that makes the crop better: higher yield, earlier maturity, more resistance. Words like susceptible or reduced resistance mark a wrong option.

items.hint1: Each weather factor has its own measuring instrument. Break the instrument's name into parts: the beginning of the word tells you what it measures.
items.hint2: Hygro- comes from a Greek word for wet or moist, and -meter means measure. So the instrument measures something to do with water in the air.
items.hint3: Wind speed has its own instrument, the anemometer, and air pressure has the barometer. Of the two factors left, which one is about moisture in the air?
items.solution:
Answer: D. relative humility

A hygrometer measures relative humidity, which is how much water vapour the air holds compared with the most it could hold at that temperature. The option says humility, a misprint for humidity. Humidity matters in farming because it affects how fast crops lose water and how easily fungal diseases spread.

How to tell: hygro- means moist and -meter means measure, so a hygrometer measures the moisture in the air.

Why not the others:
A. wind speed: measured with an anemometer.
B. daylength: hours of sunshine are recorded with a sunshine recorder.
C. atmospheric pressure: measured with a barometer.

Exam tip: learn weather instruments as pairs: rain gauge, rainfall; thermometer, temperature; hygrometer, relative humidity; anemometer, wind speed; wind vane, wind direction; barometer, air pressure; sunshine recorder, hours of sunshine.

items.hint1: Picture a hand fork being used to loosen soil in a garden. Focus on the pointed metal parts that go into the soil.
items.hint2: Some of these words name parts of other implements, and some name nothing on a fork. The correct term describes pointed parts that pierce the soil.
items.hint3: A gang is a set of discs or tines mounted together on an implement such as a harrow, so set that aside. Of the rest, which word is used for the pointed teeth of any fork?
items.solution:
Answer: D. prongs

The hand fork is a small garden tool with a short handle and three or four pointed metal fingers. These fingers are called prongs, sometimes tines. They go into the soil to loosen it, break up clods and lift out weeds.

How to tell: the finger-like parts pierce the soil, and on a fork, from a hand fork to a table fork, those pointed parts are the prongs.

Why not the others:
A. gangs: a gang is a set of discs or tines carried together on an implement such as a harrow, not a part of a hand fork.
B. rings: a hand fork has no rings as working parts.
C. rods: rods are straight bars, not the name of the pointed parts of a fork.

Exam tip: for tool-part questions, picture the tool in use and name the part that touches the soil or crop. Learn each tool's parts together with its use.

items.hint1: Watch the word not. Three options are real reasons for looking after farm machines, and one is something a farmer would not want.
items.hint2: Good maintenance keeps a machine safe, working well and lasting longer. Salvage value is the money a machine can still fetch when it is sold at the end of its useful life.
items.hint3: Preventing accidents and keeping a machine in good working condition are plainly benefits. Compare the other two: does maintenance raise or lower what the machine is worth later?
items.solution:
Answer: A. reduce the salvage value

Farm machines are maintained so that they stay safe, work well and last longer. Salvage value is what a machine can be sold for at the end of its useful life, and a well-kept machine keeps more of that value, so maintenance protects salvage value rather than reducing it.

How to tell: the question asks for the statement that is not a reason. Three options are benefits a farmer wants. Reducing salvage value would be a loss, so it cannot be a reason for maintenance.

Why not the others:
B. prolong the useful life: regular servicing slows wear, so the machine lasts longer. This is a real reason.
C. prevent avoidable accidents: checking brakes, bolts and guards cuts down accidents. This is a real reason.
D. keep in good working condition: maintenance keeps the machine ready to work when needed. This is a real reason.

Exam tip: in a not question, test each option by asking: is this a benefit? The option that describes a loss or harm is usually the answer.

items.hint1: Recall the three main groups of rocks and how each one forms. Strata means layers.
items.hint2: Strata form when particles settle out of water, one layer on top of another, over a long time. Rocks formed from cooled molten rock are not built up this way.
items.hint3: Basalt forms when lava cools quickly at the surface, and gabbro forms when molten rock cools slowly underground. Of the two left, which one is built up from shells and sediment?
items.solution:
Answer: B. limestone

Sedimentary rocks form when particles such as sand, mud or the shells of sea animals settle, usually under water, and are pressed together layer upon layer over a long time. These layers are called strata, so layering is a typical feature of sedimentary rock.

How to tell: limestone is a sedimentary rock built up from shells and calcium carbonate laid down in water, so it typically shows strata. The other three are igneous rocks, formed from cooled molten rock, and strata are not their typical feature.

Why not the others:
A. gabbro: an igneous rock that cooled slowly deep underground, made of large interlocking crystals rather than settled layers.
C. granite: an igneous rock with large crystals, not built up from settled layers.
D. basalt: an igneous rock formed when lava cools quickly at the surface. Lava flows can pile up, but they are not sedimentary strata.

Exam tip: link each feature to a rock group: layers (strata) and fossils point to sedimentary rock, crystals formed from molten rock point to igneous rock, and rock changed by heat and pressure is metamorphic.

items.hint1: Soil water is grouped by how tightly the soil holds it. Think about which kind roots can actually take up.
items.hint2: Water held very tightly as a thin film around each soil particle cannot be pulled off by roots, even though it is in the soil.
items.hint3: Rain is where soil water comes from, not a kind held in the soil. Between water that drains down quickly after rain and water held in the tiny spaces between particles, which stays long enough for roots to use?
items.solution:
Answer: C. capillary water

Soil water is grouped by how firmly the soil holds it. Capillary water is held in the small pore spaces between soil particles by surface tension, like water held in a sponge. It is held firmly enough not to drain away but loosely enough for roots to absorb, so it is the main water available to plants.

How to tell: water that plants can use must stay in the soil and also be easy for roots to take up. Capillary water does both.

Why not the others:
A. precipitation water: this is rain, the source of soil water, not a form of water held in the soil.
B. gravitational water: it drains down through the large pores soon after rain, so little of it stays for roots to use.
D. hygroscopic: this water forms a very thin film held so tightly to the particles that roots cannot pull it off.

Exam tip: remember soil water by grip: gravitational water is held too loosely, hygroscopic water too tightly, and capillary water just right for plants.

items.hint1: The dish was weighed empty and then with soil in it. To find the mass of the soil alone, think about what you must take away from the second reading.
items.hint2: Mass of soil = (mass of dish + soil) − (mass of empty dish). The line printed as dish + fresh dish means the dish with the fresh soil in it.
items.hint3: Use the fresh soil reading, not the dried soil one, and take away the dish. Work it out and find the matching option.
items.solution:
Answer: D. 60g

To get the mass of soil alone, weigh the dish with the soil in it and subtract the mass of the empty dish. This is called weighing by difference. The line printed as dish + fresh dish is a misprint for dish + fresh soil.

How to tell:
Mass of dish + fresh soil = 70 g
Mass of empty dish = 10 g
Mass of fresh soil = 70 g − 10 g = 60 g

Why not the others:
A. 15g: this is the drop between the fresh and dried readings, which is the water lost, not the soil.
B. 25g: this does not come from any correct step with these readings.
C. 45g: this is the mass of the dried soil, 55 g − 10 g, not the fresh soil.

Exam tip: in any weighing experiment, subtract the container first. Write fresh soil, dry soil and water lost on three separate lines before you answer.

items.hint1: Drying drives the water out of the soil, so the soil gets lighter. Compare two readings from the results.
items.hint2: The same dish is weighed before and after drying, so its mass cancels out. Water lost = (dish + fresh soil) − (dish + dried soil).
items.hint3: Subtract the smaller reading from the larger. Check that your answer is less than the mass of soil you started with, then pick the matching option.
items.solution:
Answer: A. 15g

In the school method, the soil is dried in an oven at about 105 °C until its mass stops falling. The drop in mass is taken as the mass of water the soil held.

How to tell:
Mass of dish + fresh soil = 70 g
Mass of dish + dried soil = 55 g
Moisture lost = 70 g − 55 g = 15 g
The dish is in both readings, so it cancels out.

Why not the others:
B. 45g: this is the mass of the dried soil, 55 g − 10 g, not the water.
C. 65g: this adds the dish to the dried reading, and it is more than the whole fresh soil, which is impossible for water lost.
D. 80g: this adds the dish to the fresh reading, and it too is more than the soil itself.

Exam tip: water lost can never be more than the fresh soil you started with. Subtract the dried reading from the fresh reading and check the answer is smaller than the fresh soil mass.

items.hint1: A percentage compares a part with a whole. Decide what the part is here and what the whole is.
items.hint2: In the school method, percentage moisture = (mass of water lost ÷ mass of fresh soil) × 100. Use soil masses with the dish taken away.
items.hint3: Some options come from the correct water figure divided by the wrong mass, such as the dried soil or a reading that still includes the dish. Make sure you divide by the fresh soil alone, then work it out.
items.solution:
Answer: B. 25%

Percentage moisture tells you what share of the soil sample, as it was collected, was water. In the school method it is worked out on the fresh soil: the water lost is the part and the fresh soil is the whole.

How to tell:
Mass of fresh soil = 70 g − 10 g = 60 g
Moisture lost = 70 g − 55 g = 15 g
Percentage moisture = (15 g ÷ 60 g) × 100
= 0.25 × 100
= 25%

Why not the others:
A. 21%: this divides 15 g by 70 g, a reading that still includes the 10 g dish.
C. 27%: this divides 15 g by 55 g, the dried reading with the dish still in it.
D. 33%: this divides 15 g by 45 g, the dried soil. Soil scientists sometimes work moisture on a dry basis, but the school formula uses the fresh soil.

Exam tip: for moisture percentage, divide the water lost by the fresh soil mass with the container removed. An option that matches water ÷ dry soil is the usual trap.

items.hint1: Think about which layer of the soil profile has the most humus, roots and living organisms, and what they do to soil particles.
items.hint2: Granular, or crumb, structure is small rounded clumps of soil held together by humus and by the work of roots, earthworms and microbes. So it forms where organic matter is highest.
items.hint3: The deepest layers are broken parent rock or solid rock, so set those aside. Between the topsoil and the subsoil, which one has more humus and soil life?
items.solution:
Answer: A. horizon A

Granular or crumb structure is made of small rounded clumps of soil. Humus, roots, earthworms and microbes bind particles into these crumbs, so this structure is typical of the layer richest in organic matter, the topsoil or A horizon.

How to tell: horizon A is the topsoil, dark with humus and full of roots and soil life. That is where crumbs form.

Why not the others:
B. horizon B: the subsoil has little humus and collects clay washed down from above, so it usually has a blocky or prismatic structure.
C. horizon C: this is weathered parent material, broken pieces of rock with little soil structure.
D. horizon D: in schemes that name it, this is the bedrock, solid rock with no soil structure.

Exam tip: link each horizon to its main feature: A, humus and crumbs; B, clay and minerals washed down from above; C, broken parent rock; below that, solid bedrock.

items.hint1: Changes in leaf colour often point to a missing nutrient. First decide which nutrient is linked to this colour, then which fertilizer supplies it.
items.hint2: In the syllabus, purple or reddish colouring of leaves, often with stunted growth, is the classic sign of phosphorus deficiency.
items.hint3: Calcium carbonate is lime, used mainly to correct acid soil. Of the three fertilizers left, look for the one whose name shows it carries the nutrient you identified.
items.solution:
Answer: C. single superphosphate

Phosphorus helps root growth, flowering and seed formation. When it is short, many crops, cowpea included, show purple or reddish leaves and stunted growth. The remedy is a fertilizer that supplies phosphorus, and single superphosphate is a phosphate fertilizer.

How to tell: purple leaves → phosphorus deficiency → a phosphate fertilizer → single superphosphate.

Why not the others:
A. calcium carbonate: this is lime, used mainly to correct soil acidity and supply calcium, not phosphorus.
B. ammonium sulphate: this supplies nitrogen, which corrects pale yellow leaves, not purple ones.
D. muriate of potash: this supplies potassium, whose shortage shows as scorched brown leaf edges.

Exam tip: learn symptom, nutrient and fertilizer as a chain: yellowing, nitrogen, urea or ammonium sulphate; purpling, phosphorus, superphosphate; scorched leaf edges, potassium, muriate of potash.

items.hint1: Agricultural pollution comes mainly from farm chemicals and animal waste getting into soil, water and air. Look for the practice that cuts down those sources.
items.hint2: Excess fertilizer and herbicide can wash into rivers and ponds, and animal waste close to water pollutes it. Look for the practice that cuts down these sources rather than adding to them.
items.hint3: A poultry farm beside a river lets droppings wash straight into the water, and inorganic fertilizer can run off into streams. Between the two options left, which one adds a chemical to the field and which one avoids it?
items.solution:
Answer: D. practicing organic farming

Agricultural pollution happens when farm chemicals, such as fertilizers, herbicides and pesticides, or animal waste get into soil, water and air in harmful amounts. Organic farming uses manure, compost, crop rotation and natural pest control instead of synthetic chemicals, so it greatly reduces the main sources of farm pollution.

How to tell: a preventive practice cuts down a source of pollution. Organic farming avoids synthetic fertilizers and pesticides, while the other three options put chemicals or waste where they can reach soil and water.

Why not the others:
A. applying inorganic fertilizers to soils: excess fertilizer washes into rivers and ponds and pollutes them.
B. spraying herbicides to control weeds: herbicide residues can poison soil, water and fish.
C. siting poultry farms near rivers: droppings and waste wash straight into the water.

Exam tip: in pollution questions, ask whether each practice adds to or cuts down the chemicals and waste that reach soil and water. The practice that cuts them down is the preventive one.

items.hint1: Crops store food in different organs: roots, stems, leaves or seeds. Think about which organ the yam tuber really is, not just where it grows.
items.hint2: A tuber that grows underground is not always a root. In the syllabus, a tuber that can produce new shoots from its tissue, as a stem does from its buds, is classed as a stem tuber.
items.hint3: A sett is a piece cut off for planting, and yam leaves are not where the plant keeps its food store. Between root and stem, recall which group yam shares with Irish potato in the storage organ list.
items.solution:
Answer: B. stem

The yam tuber grows underground, but in the syllabus it is classed as a stem tuber, a swollen underground stem that stores starch. Stems carry buds that can grow into new shoots, and yam tubers sprout new shoots, which is why pieces of tuber are planted.

How to tell: a yam tuber produces new shoots, a feature of stems. Cassava and sweet potato, by contrast, store food in swollen roots.

Why not the others:
A. root: root tubers such as cassava and sweet potato store food in roots, but the yam tuber is classed as a stem.
C. sett: a sett is a piece of yam tuber cut for planting, not the organ that stores the food.
D. leaf: yam leaves make food by photosynthesis, but the yam's food store is its tuber, not its leaves.

Exam tip: do not judge a storage organ by where it grows. Learn the pairs: root tubers, cassava and sweet potato; stem tubers, yam and Irish potato; corm, cocoyam; bulb, onion; rhizome, ginger.

items.hint1: Think about what grows on harvested produce when it is damp. The link between moisture and spoilage matters more here than the exact crop.
items.hint2: In the syllabus, nematodes are treated mainly as soil pests that attack roots in the field, and viruses multiply only inside living plant cells. Neither is the usual cause of spoilage in damp harvested grain.
items.hint3: Between the two remaining kinds of microbe, which one grows as the fluffy, coloured mould often seen on damp stored grain?
items.solution:
Answer: C. fungi

Damp grain in store is ideal for moulds, which are fungi. They rot the grain, and some, such as Aspergillus, produce aflatoxins, poisons harmful to people and animals. Letting the grain dry to a safe moisture content before harvest, and drying it further before storage, keeps moulds from growing.

How to tell: the link the syllabus teaches is high moisture in grain → mould growth → fungal contamination. Drying is the main defence.

Why not the others:
A. nematodes: in the syllabus these tiny worms are treated mainly as root pests in the field, not as the cause of mould in damp grain.
B. viruses: these multiply only inside living plant cells and are usually spread in the field by insects, not by grain moisture.
D. bacteria: they also like moisture, but in the syllabus the spoilage of damp grain is linked to moulds and aflatoxins, which are fungal.

Exam tip: in storage questions, damp produce points to moulds, which are fungi, and to aflatoxin. The remedy is drying the produce to a safe moisture content before storing it.

items.hint1: Many crop diseases are named after what they do to one particular crop. Think about which crop has branches, its arms, that turn black with this disease.
items.hint2: Blackarm is a bacterial disease, also called bacterial blight. It causes angular spots on the leaves and black, sunken marks on the stems and branches.
items.hint3: Plantain is known for Sigatoka, and citrus for canker and gummosis. Between yam and cotton, which one is attacked by a bacterial blight that blackens its branches?
items.solution:
Answer: A. cotton

Blackarm, also called bacterial blight of cotton, is caused by a bacterium, Xanthomonas. It causes angular, water-soaked spots on the leaves and black, sunken marks on the stems and branches, which is where the name black arm comes from. It can also rot the bolls and lower the yield of lint.

How to tell: in the syllabus list of bacterial diseases, blackarm belongs to cotton, just as cassava bacterial blight belongs to cassava.

Why not the others:
B. citrus: its main diseases in the syllabus are canker, gummosis and dieback, not blackarm.
C. yam: its diseases include yam mosaic and tuber rots, not blackarm.
D. plantain: its best-known disease is Sigatoka leaf spot, not blackarm.

Exam tip: learn diseases as disease, crop and cause: blackarm, cotton, bacterium; black pod, cocoa, fungus; swollen shoot, cocoa, virus; Sigatoka, banana and plantain, fungus.

items.hint1: Think about what polishing does to a rice grain: it rubs off the outer layers to leave a white, shiny grain.
items.hint2: Polishing removes material, so it cannot add to the amount of grain. It also rubs off most of the germ, the part that would grow into a new plant.
items.hint3: Between the hardness of the grain and its food value, which one changes when the brown bran layer, rich in vitamins, is rubbed off?
items.solution:
Answer: C. reduces the nutritive value of grains

Polishing rubs off the bran and most of the germ to give white, shiny rice. These parts hold much of the grain's B vitamins, minerals and fibre, and some of its protein, so polished rice is less nutritious than brown rice. People who live mainly on polished rice can suffer from beriberi, caused by lack of vitamin B₁.

How to tell: polishing only takes material away, and what it removes is the most nutritious part, so the food value falls.

Why not the others:
A. reduces the hardness of grains: polishing makes the grain smooth and white, but the grain stays hard.
B. increases the quantity of grain: removing layers makes the grain slightly lighter, not more.
D. increases the germination rate of grains: polishing removes or damages the germ, so polished rice sprouts poorly, if at all.

Exam tip: when asked for the effect of a processing step, ask what the step removes or adds, then ask what that part did. Removing the bran and germ removes nutrients.

items.hint1: Budding joins a chosen variety, the scion, to a rootstock that brings useful qualities. Think about which part of the tree the rootstock forms and protects.
items.hint2: The rootstock forms the roots and the base of the trunk, so a resistant rootstock protects against a disease that attacks the tree near soil level. Sour orange is valued for resisting a soil-borne disease.
items.hint3: Citrus scab and powdery mildew attack leaves and fruit high up the tree. Between the two diseases left, which one attacks the foot of the trunk rather than the leaves, twigs and fruit?
items.solution:
Answer: A. gummosis

Gummosis, also called foot rot, is caused by Phytophthora, a soil-borne organism that the syllabus groups with the fungi. It attacks the bark at the foot of the trunk, which cracks and oozes gum, and it can kill the tree. Sour orange resists it, so sweet orange, which is easily attacked, is budded on to sour orange rootstock: the tree gives sweet fruit on top and resists foot rot at the bottom.

How to tell: a rootstock protects the part of the tree it forms, the roots and the base of the trunk. Gummosis is the disease that attacks there.

Why not the others:
B. canker: a bacterial disease of leaves, twigs and fruit, controlled mainly by copper sprays and cutting off infected parts.
C. citrus scab: a fungal disease of young leaves and fruit, controlled by spraying fungicides.
D. powdery mildew: a fungal disease seen as a white powder on leaves, controlled with sulphur sprays.

Exam tip: when a question links budding or grafting to disease control, look for a disease of the roots or trunk base. A resistant rootstock mainly protects the parts it forms.

items.hint1: Plantation agriculture means growing one crop on a very large estate for many years. Think about which kinds of crops stay in the ground that long.
items.hint2: Plantations suit perennial tree crops that yield for many years, such as citrus, cocoa, coffee, tea, oil palm and rubber. Crops harvested within a few weeks or months are not typical plantation crops.
items.hint3: Decide which of the three groups is mainly short-season crops grown on small plots and market gardens. Then pick the option that leaves that group out.
items.solution:
Answer: B. I and III

Plantation agriculture is the large-scale growing of a single crop, usually a perennial tree crop, on an estate for many years, mainly for sale or export. In the syllabus the typical examples are fruit crops, such as citrus and banana, and beverage crops, such as cocoa, coffee and tea.

How to tell: fruits (I) and beverages (III) include long-lived tree crops, which fit plantations. Vegetables (II) are short-season crops usually grown on small farms and market gardens, so they are left out.

Why not the others:
A. I and II: includes vegetables, which are not typical plantation crops, and leaves out beverages, which are.
C. II and III: includes vegetables and leaves out fruit crops such as citrus.
D. I, II and III: large vegetable farms do exist, but vegetables are not the crops the syllabus links with plantation agriculture.

Exam tip: for plantation questions, think of perennial tree crops grown on big estates for sale: cocoa, oil palm, rubber, citrus, coffee and tea. Short-season food crops are the usual wrong option.

items.hint1: Seed dormancy often happens because the seed coat is too hard for water to get in. Think about what would soften or crack that coat.
items.hint2: Soil treatment is aimed at pests and diseases in the soil, and sterilization is aimed at killing germs. Neither one opens a hard seed coat.
items.hint3: Between the two options left, which one softens or cracks a hard seed coat, and which one the syllabus uses to keep seeds resting safely in store?
items.solution:
Answer: C. heat treatment

Dormancy is a resting state in which a healthy seed will not germinate even when conditions are right. In many tropical seeds, especially legumes, it comes from a hard seed coat that keeps water out. Heat treatment, such as soaking seeds briefly in hot water, softens or cracks the coat so water can enter and germination can start.

How to tell: the dormancy-breaking methods the syllabus teaches, heat or hot water, scarification, soaking and acid, all open up the seed coat. Heat treatment is the one of these among the options.

Why not the others:
A. soil treatment: treating soil controls pests and diseases and does not open the seed coat.
B. refrigeration: in the syllabus, low temperature is used to store seeds and keep them resting, not to wake them. Cold treatment does break dormancy in some temperate seeds, but that is not the method this syllabus teaches.
D. sterilization: this kills germs on seeds or in soil and does not end dormancy.

Exam tip: for dormancy questions, look for a method that lets water through the seed coat: hot water, heat, scarification, soaking or acid. Methods for killing pests or germs are distractors.

items.hint1: Nitrogen-fixing trees are usually legumes, whose roots carry nodules with bacteria that turn nitrogen from the air into plant food. Check which botanical name belongs to a legume.
items.hint2: Alley cropping grows food crops between rows of fast-growing trees that are cut back often, and the cuttings are used as mulch and green manure. Big timber trees do not suit this.
items.hint3: Tectona grandis is teak, a timber tree. Of the other three names, one is a legume widely planted in hedgerows. Which do you recognise from your agroforestry lessons?
items.solution:
Answer: B. Leucaena leucocephala

Leucaena is a fast-growing leguminous tree. Like other legumes, it has root nodules containing Rhizobium bacteria, which fix nitrogen from the air. In alley cropping, food crops are grown in the alleys between hedgerows of Leucaena, and the hedgerows are pruned so the leaves can be used as mulch and green manure, adding nitrogen and organic matter to the soil.

How to tell: among these options, Leucaena is the only legume, and, like Gliricidia, it is the standard nitrogen-fixing example for alley cropping in the syllabus.

Why not the others:
A. Tectona grandis: teak, a timber tree that is not a legume and does not fix nitrogen.
C. Terminalia superba: afara, a timber tree that is not a legume.
D. Tertulia Africana: most likely a misprint for Treculia africana, the African breadfruit, which is not a legume and does not fix nitrogen.

Exam tip: nitrogen fixing usually points to a legume. For agroforestry and alley cropping questions, remember Leucaena and Gliricidia as the hedgerow legumes.

items.hint1: Ornamental plants are grouped by form: trees, shrubs, climbers, grasses and flowers. Picture Allamanda, the plant with large bright yellow trumpet-shaped flowers seen in school and home gardens.
items.hint2: A seed is a planting material, not a form of plant, so it cannot describe an ornamental plant.
items.hint3: Grasses have narrow leaves with parallel veins, which Allamanda does not have. Between a tree and a shrub, compare Allamanda's usual height and stem arrangement with the features of those two forms.
items.solution:
Answer: C. shrub

Allamanda (Allamanda cathartica) is a woody ornamental plant with glossy leaves and large yellow trumpet-shaped flowers. It grows as a bushy shrub with several stems from near the ground and can also be trained to climb a fence or wall, so it is used in hedges, borders and on fences.

How to tell: it has no single tall trunk like a tree, and it is woody, not a grass. Its bushy, many-stemmed form is that of a shrub.

Why not the others:
A. tree: trees such as flamboyant (Delonix) have a single tall trunk, and Allamanda does not.
B. grass: ornamental grasses such as Cynodon are used for lawns, while Allamanda is a woody flowering plant.
D. seed: a seed is a planting material, not a type of ornamental plant.

Exam tip: learn ornamental examples by form: trees, flamboyant and royal palm; shrubs, Allamanda, Hibiscus, Ixora and Croton; lawn grasses, Cynodon and carpet grass.

items.hint1: A fungicide is a chemical made to kill fungi. First decide what kind of organism causes each of these diseases.
items.hint2: Fungicides have no effect on viruses. Virus diseases are controlled with resistant varieties, by removing sick plants and by killing the insects that spread them.
items.hint3: Cassava mosaic is spread by whiteflies and cocoa swollen shoot by mealybugs. Between cotton leaf curl and Sigatoka of banana, which one is caused by the kind of organism a fungicide kills?
items.solution:
Answer: D. sigatoka diseases of banana

A fungicide is a chemical that kills or stops fungi, so it is used against diseases caused by fungi. Sigatoka of banana and plantain is caused by a fungus, Mycosphaerella, which makes streaks and spots on the leaves until they dry out, so regular fungicide spraying controls it.

How to tell: sort the diseases by cause. Three are virus diseases spread by insects, and Sigatoka is the one caused by a fungus.

Why not the others:
A. cassava mosaic: a virus disease spread by whiteflies, controlled with resistant varieties and clean cuttings.
B. swollen shoot of cocoa: a virus disease spread by mealybugs, controlled by cutting out infected trees and controlling the mealybugs.
C. cotton leaf curl: a virus disease spread by whiteflies, controlled with resistant varieties and by controlling the insects.

Exam tip: match the chemical to the cause: fungicides for fungi, insecticides for insects and for the insects that carry viruses, nematicides for nematodes. Words like mosaic, swollen shoot and leaf curl usually point to a virus.

items.hint1: A plant's seeds are spread in a way that suits its fruit. Think about the fruit of waterleaf, a common weed in Nigerian farms: is it fleshy, winged, hooked, or a small dry case?
items.hint2: Seeds spread by animals usually have hooks or a fleshy covering, wind-spread seeds have wings or hairs, and water-spread seeds have floats. Waterleaf seeds are tiny, smooth and black, with none of these.
items.hint3: Running water and wind suit seeds with floats or wings, which waterleaf lacks. Between animals and the fruit itself, which is more likely to scatter seeds that have no hooks or flesh?
items.solution:
Answer: D. explosive mechanisms

Talinum triangulare, waterleaf, produces its seeds in small dry capsules. When ripe, a capsule splits open and flings out many tiny seeds around the parent plant. In the syllabus weed tables, this is classed as dispersal by an explosive mechanism.

How to tell: the seeds have no hooks, flesh, wings, hairs or floats, so none of the carrying agents suits them. The dry capsule that bursts open is the plant's own way of spreading them.

Why not the others:
A. animals: animal-spread seeds have hooks or a sweet fleshy covering, and waterleaf seeds have neither.
B. running water: rain can wash the tiny seeds along, but that is not the main method, and they have no floats.
C. wind: wind-spread seeds have wings or hairs, while waterleaf seeds are smooth.

Exam tip: for dispersal questions, read the fruit or seed: hooks or flesh, animals; wings or hairs, wind; spongy or fibrous floats, water; dry pods or capsules that split open, explosive.

items.hint1: Cattle breeds are grouped by their main use: beef, milk, work, or both beef and milk. Dual-purpose means kept for two main products.
items.hint2: Muturu is a small, humpless breed kept mainly for beef and valued because it tolerates trypanosomiasis. It gives little milk.
items.hint3: Red Bororo, the large deep-red zebu, is kept mainly for beef. Between Keteku, a crossbred breed, and White Fulani, which breed is known for giving milk as well as beef?
items.solution:
Answer: C. white Fulani

A dual-purpose breed is kept for two main products, usually milk and beef. White Fulani (Bunaji), a humped zebu breed with a white coat, is the standard Nigerian example: it gives a fair amount of milk and also a good carcass for beef.

How to tell: of the local breeds listed, White Fulani is the one the syllabus names for both milk and meat.

Why not the others:
A. muturu: a small, humpless breed kept mainly for beef, which tolerates trypanosomiasis but gives little milk.
B. keteku: a cross between humpless West African cattle and zebu cattle, kept mainly for beef and work.
D. red Bororo: a large, deep-red zebu breed kept mainly for beef, with little milk.

Exam tip: group breeds by main use: beef, Muturu, N'dama and Red Bororo; dairy, Friesian and Jersey; dual-purpose, White Fulani.

items.hint1: Some products can be collected while the animal stays alive, and others come only after it is killed. Sort each product into one of these two groups.
items.hint2: Chevon is the name for goat meat, just as mutton is the meat of sheep and pork is the meat of pigs.
items.hint3: Decide whether chevon can come from a living goat. Then check whether eggs and milk can come from living animals, and pick the option that matches.
items.solution:
Answer: B. I and III

Products from living animals are collected without killing the animal, so it goes on producing. Hens lay eggs, and cows and goats are milked. Meat, on the other hand, comes only from a slaughtered animal.

How to tell: chevon (II) is goat meat, so it needs slaughter. Eggs (I) and milk (III) come from living animals.

Why not the others:
A. I and II: includes chevon, which is obtained only after slaughter.
C. II and III: includes chevon and leaves out eggs.
D. I, II and III: includes chevon.

Exam tip: learn the meat names: beef from cattle, veal from calves, mutton from sheep, chevon from goats, pork from pigs. Meat, hides, horns and hooves come after slaughter; milk, eggs, wool and dung come from living animals.

items.hint1: Follow undigested feed along the gut after the stomachs. Think about which section's main job is to take back water before faeces are formed.
items.hint2: Digestion and absorption of nutrients happen mainly in the small intestine. Water is taken back mainly in the large intestine, before the faeces leave the body.
items.hint3: The duodenum is part of the small intestine, and the rectum mainly holds faeces until they are passed out. Between the caecum and the colon, which one has water absorption as its main job?
items.solution:
Answer: D. colon

After nutrients have been absorbed in the small intestine, the leftover undigested feed passes into the large intestine. In the colon, most of the remaining water is absorbed back into the body, so the residue becomes firmer faeces and the animal does not lose too much water.

How to tell: in the syllabus, absorbing water from undigested material is the main job of the colon.

Why not the others:
A. caecum: a blind pouch where microbes ferment fibre; it absorbs some water, but that is not its main job.
B. rectum: it mainly stores faeces until they are passed out.
C. duodenum: the first part of the small intestine, where feed is digested, not where water is taken back from waste.

Exam tip: match each gut part to one main job: rumen, fermentation; abomasum, true stomach digestion; small intestine, nutrient absorption; caecum, fermentation; colon, water absorption; rectum, storing faeces.

items.hint1: This is an except question. Check each statement against what the rumen actually does, and look for the one that is not a rumen function.
items.hint2: The rumen is the largest stomach compartment. Feed is held there for a while and brought back up to be chewed again, and microbes in it break down fibre by fermentation.
items.hint3: Rumen microbes do make certain vitamins, but not all of them. Recall where a cow gets vitamins A and D, then decide whether statement III is true.
items.solution:
Answer: C. III only

The rumen stores feed for a time and ferments it with microbes, which break down fibre. Those microbes also make B-complex vitamins and vitamin K, but not vitamins A and D. Vitamin A comes from carotene in green feed, and vitamin D is made in the skin in sunlight or comes from the feed.

How to tell: I, storage, is true and II, fermentation, is true, so both are functions. III is false, so it is the exception.

Why not the others:
A. I only: storage is a real function of the rumen, so I is not the exception.
B. II only: fermentation is the rumen's main function, so II is not the exception.
D. I and III: III is an exception, but I is a real function, so this option is wrong.

Exam tip: in except questions with Roman numerals, mark each statement true or false first, then pick the option that lists exactly the false ones.

items.hint1: Watch the word not. Collecting semen means getting it from the male. Think about the steps of artificial insemination and which tool belongs to a different step.
items.hint2: Artificial insemination has two main steps: collecting semen from the male, then placing it in the female's reproductive tract. The tools for the two steps are different.
items.hint3: An artificial vagina and electro-ejaculation are both used on the male. Between massage and use of a catheter, decide which one acts on the male to make him release semen.
items.solution:
Answer: C. use of catheter

In artificial insemination, semen is first collected from the male and then placed in the female. The collection methods are the artificial vagina, which the male mounts, massage, and electro-ejaculation, where a mild electric current makes the male release semen. A catheter, or insemination tube, is a thin tube used in the second step, to place semen into the female.

How to tell: a catheter puts semen in rather than getting it out, so it is not a collection method.

Why not the others:
A. use of artificial vagina: a warm, lined tube the male mounts, the standard collection method for bulls and rams.
B. massage: stroking the cock's abdomen, or massaging the glands through the rectum wall in bulls, makes the male release semen.
D. electro ejaculation: a mild electric current from a probe in the rectum makes the male release semen, useful when the male cannot mount.

Exam tip: in artificial insemination questions, sort each tool by step: collecting (artificial vagina, massage, electro-ejaculation), storing (liquid nitrogen) and inseminating (catheter or insemination gun).

items.hint1: Think about what a hot animal does to cool itself down, and how that changes what it eats and drinks.
items.hint2: An animal under heat stress eats less, because digesting food makes body heat, and it drinks more to replace water lost in cooling. Any option that says the opposite can go.
items.hint3: With less feed going in, which output of the animal is likely to fall?
items.solution:
Answer: D. reduced milk production

Heat stress happens when an animal cannot lose body heat fast enough. It eats less, because digesting feed produces more heat, and with less feed coming in it has fewer nutrients to turn into products such as milk.

How to tell: heat stress lowers feed intake. Milk is made from the nutrients in feed, so a cow that eats less in hot weather gives less milk.

Why not the others:
A. increased feed intake: heat-stressed animals eat less, not more.
B. reduced water intake: they drink more water to replace what they lose through panting and sweating.
C. increased little size: this means litter size, the number of young born at once, and heat stress tends to lower it by harming fertility.

Exam tip: for heat stress questions, remember the pattern: feed intake down, water intake up, and growth, milk, eggs and fertility down.

items.hint1: In stocking questions, first find how much floor space the whole house gives you.
items.hint2: The floor area of a rectangular house is length × breadth. The number of birds is that area shared out at the space each bird needs.
items.hint3: Divide the floor area you found by the 0.36 m² each bird needs. Multiplying both numbers by 100 first turns it into a division by 36. Which option matches?
items.solution:
Answer: D. 500

Each bird needs a fixed amount of floor space, so the number of birds a house can hold is its total floor area divided by the space for one bird. (The question says "children", but it means chickens.)

How to tell:
Floor area = 9 m × 20 m = 180 m²
Space per bird = 0.36 m²
Number of birds = 180 m² ÷ 0.36 m²
= 18,000 ÷ 36
= 500 birds

Why not the others:
A. 65: far too few, since 65 birds would use only about 23 m² of the 180 m² floor.
B. 81: also far too few, since 81 birds would use only about 29 m² of the floor.
C. 180: this is the floor area in m², not the number of birds.

Exam tip: for any stocking sum, work out the total area first, then divide by the space for one animal. If an option equals the area itself, it is a trap.

items.hint1: Think about the climate in West Africa and what poultry need most from their house in hot, humid weather.
items.hint2: Open sides let things move freely in and out of the house. They do not block wind or hold warmth in, so options about shelter from wind or warmth do not fit.
items.hint3: Of the two options left, one is about the air in the house and one is about the floor. Which one do open sides actually affect?
items.solution:
Answer: C. promotes adequate ventilation

In a hot, humid climate, poultry make a lot of heat, moisture and ammonia from their droppings. Open sides, usually covered with wire mesh, let fresh air flow through the house and carry these away.

How to tell: the open sides change how air moves. Good airflow is called ventilation, and it keeps the birds cool, keeps the litter drier and lowers the risk of disease.

Why not the others:
A. protect birds from strong winds: open sides let wind in, which is why they are fitted with curtains or low walls for protection.
B. keep the bird warm: open sides let heat escape, which is the opposite of keeping birds warm.
D. facilitates easy cleaning: cleaning depends on the floor and the litter, not on whether the sides are open.

Exam tip: when a question asks why a poultry house is built a certain way in the tropics, think about heat and air first. Open sides, high roofs and an east to west layout all help ventilation and cooling.

items.hint1: Each option is the name for a male of one kind of farm animal. First work out which animal each name belongs to.
items.hint2: Wool is the fleece, the soft coat that is sheared off each year. In the syllabus it comes from one kind of farm animal.
items.hint3: Which animal gives wool, and which of the four names is the male of that animal?
items.solution:
Answer: C. ram

In the syllabus, wool is the fleece of sheep. A ram is a male sheep, so wool can be obtained from a ram.

How to tell: match each name to its animal. Boar is a male pig, buck is a male goat or rabbit, ram is a male sheep, and cock is a male fowl. In the syllabus, wool comes from sheep.

Why not the others:
A. boar: a male pig, which has coarse bristles, not wool.
B. buck: a male goat or rabbit; the syllabus links wool with sheep, not with these animals.
D. cock: a male fowl, which has feathers.

Exam tip: learn the male, female and young names for each farm animal, such as ram, ewe and lamb for sheep, and boar, sow and piglet for pigs. Many product questions hide the animal behind one of these names.

items.hint1: Start by asking what kind of organism causes each of the three diseases.
items.hint2: In the syllabus, sulphur drugs are used against diseases caused by protozoa and fungi. Diseases caused by viruses are controlled by vaccination rather than cured with drugs.
items.hint3: One of the three diseases is caused by a virus. Find it, then cross out every option that still includes it.
items.solution:
Answer: A. I and II

In the syllabus, sulphur-containing drugs are used against diseases caused by protozoa and fungi. Coccidiosis is caused by a protozoan and is treated with sulpha drugs (sulphonamides). Ringworm is caused by a fungus and is treated with sulphur-based ointments on the skin. Fowl pox is caused by a virus, and drugs do not cure it.

How to tell: sort by cause. Coccidiosis is protozoan, ringworm is fungal and fowl pox is viral. Fowl pox is prevented by vaccination, so it drops out, leaving I and II.

Why not the others:
B. I and III: fowl pox is viral and is not treated with sulphur drugs.
C. II and III: it includes fowl pox and leaves out coccidiosis, the disease sulpha drugs are best known for.
D. I, II and III: it includes fowl pox, which is controlled by vaccination.

Exam tip: in treatment questions, name the cause first. Viral diseases such as fowl pox and Newcastle disease are prevented by vaccination, while protozoan and fungal diseases can be treated with drugs.

items.hint1: The question says "most important". Think about which benefit of bees reaches the most farms and the most food, not only the hive.
items.hint2: Bees give products from the hive, but they also do work outside the hive as they visit flowers. Research use is a small benefit and can be set aside.
items.hint3: Compare the value of what bees make in the hive with the value of what they do for crops in the field. Which is bigger?
items.solution:
Answer: C. act as agent of pollination

As bees move from flower to flower, they carry pollen, which lets many fruit, vegetable and seed crops form fruits and seeds. Textbooks give this as the most important function of bees, because its value to crop production is far greater than the value of hive products.

How to tell: "most important" asks for the biggest benefit. Pollination raises the harvest of whole farms, while beeswax and other hive products come from the hive alone.

Why not the others:
A. produce beeswax: a real bee product, but worth far less than pollination.
B. provide raw materials: hive products do serve as raw materials, but again this is secondary to pollination.
D. be used for research purposes: a minor use that affects few people.

Exam tip: when a question asks for the "most important" or "main" role, several options may be true. Pick the one with the widest effect on farming and food supply.

items.hint1: Split the options into crops grown mainly for food at home and crops grown mainly to sell abroad.
items.hint2: Major export crops are cash crops grown mainly for sale abroad, while staple food crops are eaten mainly in the country where they are grown.
items.hint3: Which option is a cash crop that West African countries are well known for selling to other countries?
items.solution:
Answer: B. cocoa

An export crop is grown mainly to be sold to other countries, earning foreign exchange. Cocoa is one of West Africa's major export crops, grown in large amounts in Côte d'Ivoire, Ghana and Nigeria and sold abroad to make chocolate and other products.

How to tell: cocoa beans are grown mainly for sale overseas, while the other three are mainly eaten at home.

Why not the others:
A. maize: mainly a food and feed crop used within West Africa.
C. yam: a staple food crop mostly eaten locally.
D. plantain: a staple food crop mostly eaten locally.

Exam tip: for export crop questions, look for cash crops such as cocoa, rubber, cotton, oil palm produce, coffee, groundnut and cashew. Staple foods are usually the distractors.

items.hint1: Read the passage and pick out only the figures that belong to producing the eggs, not to selling them.
items.hint2: Cost of production per tray is the total cost of production divided by the number of trays produced. Money spent on selling is a marketing cost, not a production cost.
items.hint3: Divide ₦350,000.00 by the number of trays the farmer produced, and match your answer to the options.
items.solution:
Answer: B. ₦700.00

The cost of producing one unit is the total cost of production shared equally over all the units produced. Every tray produced counts, whether it is later sold or eaten at home.

How to tell:
Total cost of production = ₦350,000.00
Trays produced = 500
Cost per tray = ₦350,000.00 ÷ 500
= ₦700.00 per tray

Why not the others:
A. ₦640.00: this takes the ₦30,000.00 marketing cost away before dividing, but marketing is extra spending, so it cannot lower the production cost.
C. ₦760.00: this adds the ₦30,000.00 marketing cost, which is spent on selling, not on producing.
D. ₦1,000.00: this is sales money divided by trays, which is income, not cost.

Exam tip: in farm account sums, sort each figure first: production cost, marketing cost, sales, and home use. Then use only the figures the question asks about.

items.hint1: Find in the passage what happened to the eggs before any were sold.
items.hint2: Trays sold = trays produced minus trays used at home. The home use is given as a percentage of the total output.
items.hint3: Work out 1% of 500 trays, then take that away from 500.
items.solution:
Answer: C. 495

The trays sold are what is left of the total output after the family's own use has been taken out.

How to tell:
Total output = 500 trays
Family use = 1% of 500 = 500 ÷ 100 = 5 trays
Trays sold = 500 − 5 = 495 trays

Why not the others:
A. 4000: far more than the 500 trays produced, so it is impossible.
B. 490: this takes away 10 trays, which would be 2% of the output, not 1%.
D. 500: this is the total output and ignores the trays the family ate.

Exam tip: when a passage says some produce was used at home before sale, always take it away from the total before counting what was sold.

items.hint1: List every cost and every source of income in the passage, and note which figures the options seem to be built from.
items.hint2: Total cost includes both the production cost and the marketing cost. Produce eaten by the farmer's family is also counted as income. For this question, value those trays at the full cost of each tray.
items.hint3: Find the full cost of one tray (production plus marketing, shared over all trays), value the family's trays at that price, add it to the sales, and then take away the total cost.
items.solution:
Answer: B. ₦123,800.00

Net profit = total income − total cost. In farm accounts, produce the family eats is still part of what the farm produced, so it is counted as income even though no money changed hands. In this question it is valued at the full cost per tray.

How to tell:
Total cost = ₦350,000.00 + ₦30,000.00 = ₦380,000.00
Full cost per tray = ₦380,000.00 ÷ 500 = ₦760.00
Trays eaten by the family = 1% of 500 = 5 trays
Value of home use = 5 × ₦760.00 = ₦3,800.00
Total income = ₦500,000.00 + ₦3,800.00 = ₦503,800.00
Net profit = ₦503,800.00 − ₦380,000.00 = ₦123,800.00

Why not the others:
A. ₦120,000.00: this takes the costs away from sales but leaves out the value of the eggs the family ate.
C. ₦150,000.00: this leaves out both the marketing cost and the home use.
D. ₦153,800.00: this counts the home use but leaves out the ₦30,000.00 marketing cost.

Exam tip: in net profit sums, include every cost, and count home use as income. If a small odd figure such as ₦3,800 appears in several options, the setter expects you to include home use.

items.hint1: Think about what makes a buyer willing to pay more for farm produce.
items.hint2: A buyer pays more when the produce is wanted by many people, when it is of a known, good quality, or when it has been turned into a more useful form. Check each of the three against these.
items.hint3: Test I, II and III one at a time against the idea in hint 2: does telling more buyers about the produce fit, does sorting it into quality grades fit, does turning it into another product fit? Combine only the ones you find actually fit.
items.solution:
Answer: D. I, II and III

Marketing functions are the activities that move produce from the farm to the buyer. Several of them can raise the price a farmer can ask, because they make the produce more wanted, more trusted or more useful.

How to tell: advertisement tells buyers about the produce and can increase demand. Processing can turn raw produce into a form that keeps longer or is more useful, such as cassava into garri, so it can sell for more. Grading sorts produce into quality classes, so the best grade can sell at a higher price. All three can help the farmer get a better price.

Why not the others:
A. I and II: it leaves out grading, which lets top-quality produce earn a top price.
B. I and III: it leaves out processing, which adds value to the produce.
C. II and III: it leaves out advertisement, which can raise demand and so support a better price.

Exam tip: for "which marketing functions" questions, test each listed function on its own against what the stem asks. Choose "all of them" when every one passes.
